kinematics_equations.hook: You throw a ball straight up. At the very top, its velocity is zero — but what about its acceleration? Most students say zero too. Predict, then we'll check.
kinematics_equations.recall: Write the three equations of motion for constant acceleration.
kinematics_equations.answer: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as

projectile_motion.hook: Fire a bullet horizontally and drop an identical one from the same height at the same instant. Which hits the ground first? Bet you'll be surprised — guess first.
projectile_motion.recall: Why do the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile not affect each other?
projectile_motion.answer: they're independent — horizontal velocity is constant, vertical has g; only time is shared

newtons_second_law.hook: Push a shopping cart, then push a loaded truck with the same force. The cart flies, the truck barely moves. F is the same — so what actually changed? Name it before I tell you.
newtons_second_law.recall: State Newton's second law in its most useful form.
newtons_second_law.answer: F_net = ma (or F = dp/dt) — net force equals rate of change of momentum

friction.hook: A block sits still on a slope. No one's pushing it, yet gravity pulls it down the incline. What's holding it? And why does it suddenly slip past a certain angle? Predict the trick.
friction.recall: How does static friction differ from kinetic friction, and which is larger?
friction.answer: static self-adjusts up to μ_s N and is larger; kinetic is fixed at μ_k N once sliding starts

work_energy_theorem.hook: You carry a heavy bag across a flat room and put it down. Physics says you did ZERO work on it. Feels wrong, right? Guess why before I explain.
work_energy_theorem.recall: State the work-energy theorem in one line.
work_energy_theorem.answer: net work done on a body = change in its kinetic energy (W_net = ΔKE)

circular_motion.hook: A car turns a corner at steady speed — speedometer never changes. Yet it IS accelerating. How can something at constant speed accelerate? Take a guess.
circular_motion.recall: What is centripetal acceleration, and which way does it point?
circular_motion.answer: a = v²/r, directed toward the centre — it changes direction, not speed

rotational_inertia.hook: A solid disc and a hollow ring of the SAME mass and radius roll down a ramp. One wins the race every time. Which — and why? Predict before we roll them.
rotational_inertia.recall: What does moment of inertia tell you, and what does it depend on?
rotational_inertia.answer: it's rotational mass — resistance to angular acceleration; depends on mass AND how far it's spread from the axis

gravitation.hook: Astronauts float in the ISS — everyone says 'no gravity in space'. But gravity up there is nearly as strong as on the ground. So why do they float? Guess the real reason.
gravitation.recall: State Newton's law of universal gravitation.
gravitation.answer: F = G m₁m₂ / r² — attraction ∝ product of masses, ∝ 1/distance squared

simple_harmonic_motion.hook: Pull a spring twice as far and let go. Does it take twice as long to come back? Almost everyone says yes. Predict, then we'll test it.
simple_harmonic_motion.recall: What is the defining condition for simple harmonic motion?
simple_harmonic_motion.answer: restoring force ∝ displacement and opposite to it (a = -ω²x); period is independent of amplitude

thermodynamics_first_law.hook: You can heat a gas without a flame — just by squeezing it fast. Where does that heat come from if nothing burned? Take a guess.
thermodynamics_first_law.recall: State the first law of thermodynamics.
thermodynamics_first_law.answer: ΔU = Q − W — heat added minus work done by the gas changes its internal energy

kinetic_theory.hook: Temperature isn't really 'hotness' — it's secretly measuring something the molecules are doing. What single thing does temperature actually measure? Guess before I reveal it.
kinetic_theory.recall: In kinetic theory, what does absolute temperature measure?
kinetic_theory.answer: average kinetic energy of the molecules (½mv²_avg ∝ T); KE_avg = (3/2)kT

coulombs_law.hook: Two charges attract with force F. Now double the distance between them. Is the new force half? Most guess half — it's not even close. Predict.
coulombs_law.recall: State Coulomb's law and how force scales with distance.
coulombs_law.answer: F = k q₁q₂ / r² — doubling r cuts force to one QUARTER (inverse-square)

gauss_law.hook: Stand inside a hollow charged metal sphere. There's charge all around you — yet the electric field where you stand is exactly ZERO. How can that be? Guess the reason.
gauss_law.recall: What does Gauss's law relate, and why is it powerful?
gauss_law.answer: net flux through a closed surface = q_enclosed/ε₀; only enclosed charge matters — exploits symmetry to find E fast

ohms_law.hook: You double a wire's length AND double its thickness. Does its resistance stay the same? It feels like it should cancel out — predict before we check.
ohms_law.recall: State Ohm's law and what resistance depends on.
ohms_law.answer: V = IR; R = ρL/A — grows with length, falls with cross-section area

magnetic_lorentz_force.hook: Shoot a charged particle straight along a magnetic field line. How much does the field push it? Everyone expects a big kick — the real answer surprises people. Guess.
magnetic_lorentz_force.recall: Write the magnetic force on a moving charge and when it's zero.
magnetic_lorentz_force.answer: F = qv × B — max when v ⊥ B, ZERO when v is parallel to B; force never does work (always ⊥ to v)

electromagnetic_induction.hook: Hold a magnet perfectly still inside a coil — strong field, but the voltmeter reads zero. Move it and voltage appears. So what actually creates the voltage? Predict.
electromagnetic_induction.recall: State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
electromagnetic_induction.answer: induced EMF = − rate of change of magnetic flux (ε = −dΦ/dt); it's the CHANGE that matters, not the field itself

lenz_law.hook: Drop a strong magnet down a copper pipe. It falls in slow motion, like through honey — copper isn't even magnetic. What's braking it? Guess before I explain.
lenz_law.recall: What does Lenz's law tell you about the direction of induced current?
lenz_law.answer: induced current opposes the change that caused it — it's conservation of energy in disguise

refraction_lens.hook: A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the surface — but the straw is perfectly straight. What's actually bending? Take a guess before we trace the rays.
refraction_lens.recall: Why does light bend when entering a denser medium, and which way?
refraction_lens.answer: its speed drops, so it bends TOWARD the normal (Snell's law: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂)

wave_interference.hook: Shine light through two tiny slits and you'd expect two bright lines. Instead you get many bright and DARK bands — light plus light making darkness. How? Predict the mechanism.
wave_interference.recall: What condition on path difference gives a bright fringe in Young's double-slit?
wave_interference.answer: path difference = nλ (whole wavelengths) → constructive; (n+½)λ → dark (destructive)

photoelectric_effect.hook: Shine a super-bright red lamp on a metal — no electrons come out, no matter how bright. A dim blue light ejects them instantly. Brightness loses to colour. Why? Guess.
photoelectric_effect.recall: What does the photoelectric effect prove about light, and what sets the electron's energy?
photoelectric_effect.answer: light is quantised in photons (E = hf); frequency (not intensity) must exceed the work function ϕ — KE_max = hf − ϕ
